title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement: Implement a class with insert(word), search(word) returning whether the exact word was inserted, and startsWith(prefix) returning whether any inserted word begins with prefix.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet answers exact search, but startsWith would scan every word (or store every prefix).
A sorted list supports prefix lookups in O(L log n), but inserts are O(n).
It is a class, but the one structure that fits all three operations is a trie.

trigger.why: Prefix queries over a dictionary ⇒ trie: one node per character, shared prefixes share nodes.

ds.answer: TrieNode with TrieNode[26] children and a boolean isWord
wrong: HashMap<String, Integer> prefix → count of every prefix
ds.why: The prefix-count map works but stores O(L²) characters per word.

invariant.answer: The path from the root to a node spells exactly the prefix that node represents; isWord marks where an inserted word ends.
wrong: Each node stores a whole word.
Children are sorted by insertion time.
A node exists only for complete words.
invariant.why: search needs isWord at the end node; startsWith only needs the node to exist.

time.answer: O(L) per operation, L = word length
time.why: One step per character, independent of how many words are stored.

space.why: Each new character may add a node with 26 child slots.

wrong: A HashSet can't tell whether a word was inserted.

approach: insert: walk/create child nodes per char, mark isWord. search: walk; return node != null && node.isWord. startsWith: walk; return node != null.

title: Word Search II
statement: Given a grid of letters and a list of words, return all words that can be formed from sequentially adjacent cells (no cell reused within a word).

nearMiss.why: Running Word Search once per word repeats the same grid walks; one DFS guided by a trie prunes all words at once.
A HashSet of words can't tell you to stop early when the current path isn't a prefix of any word.
Flood fill marks cells permanently; paths here must release cells on the way back.

wrong: no cell reused within a word
trigger.why: Many words searched at once over the same grid ⇒ build a trie of the words and DFS the grid, following trie edges.

ds.answer: Trie of the words (TrieNode[26] + String word at end nodes) + backtracking DFS on the board
wrong: HashSet<String> of words checked at every step
boolean[][] visited that is never reset
ds.why: The trie node you're at says which letters can continue any word.

invariant.answer: During DFS, the current trie node corresponds exactly to the letters on the current grid path; if the child for the next letter is null, that branch is cut.
wrong: Visited cells stay marked for later words.
The trie is rebuilt for every starting cell.
invariant.why: Clearing a found word (set word = null) avoids duplicates; pruning emptied nodes speeds it up.

time.answer: O(rows × cols × 3ᴸ) worst case, L = longest word
time.why: One DFS per cell, bounded by the longest word; independent of the number of words in the worst case.

wrong: Backtracking only finds the first word.
Backtracking needs the word list sorted.

approach: Insert all words into a trie (store the word at its end node). DFS from each cell following trie children, marking the cell; when node.word != null add it and null it; restore the cell.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement: Design a structure with addWord(word) and search(pattern), where the pattern may contain '.' that matches any single letter. search returns true if any added word matches.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet handles exact lookups, but '.' would force checking every stored word.
Patterns match whole words, not windows inside a string.
Wildcard DP is for '*' patterns against one string; here '.' is one letter and there are many words.

trigger.why: Character-by-character matching over many words, with branching on '.' ⇒ trie + DFS over children at wildcards.

ds.answer: TrieNode[26] trie with recursive search that tries every child on '.'
wrong: HashSet<String> plus regex matching for each word
HashMap<Integer, List<String>> length → words scanned linearly
ds.why: Bucketing by length helps but still scans words; the trie shares prefixes.

invariant.answer: search(node, i) is true iff some word below node matches pattern[i..].
wrong: '.' matches the empty string as well.
search stops at the first child it tries.
Every node marks the end of a word.
invariant.why: At '.', OR over all non-null children; at a letter, follow one child.

time.answer: addWord O(L); search O(L) without dots, up to O(26ᵈ · L) with d dots
time.why: Wildcards branch into up to 26 children each.

wrong: Hash sets can't store words with dots.
A HashSet can't add words after creation.

approach: addWord: standard trie insert. search(node, i): if i == len return node.isWord; c = pattern[i]; if '.', try every child; else follow child c.

title: LRU Cache
statement: Design a cache with a fixed capacity supporting get(key) and put(key, value), both in O(1) average time. When full, put evicts the least recently used key.

nearMiss.why: A heap by last-used time gives O(log n) and can't update a key's recency in O(1).
A HashMap gives O(1) lookup but has no notion of recency order.
A doubly linked list keeps recency order, but finding a key in it is O(n) without a map.

trigger.answer: evicts the least recently used key
trigger.why: O(1) lookup AND O(1) reorder/evict ⇒ combine a HashMap with a doubly linked list (or LinkedHashMap with accessOrder).

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Node> + doubly linked list with dummy head/tail (or LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true)
ds.why: The map finds the node; the list moves/removes it in O(1). The deque can't remove from the middle in O(1).

invariant.answer: The list is ordered from most to least recently used, and the map holds exactly the keys in the list.
wrong: The list is sorted by key.
The map may contain evicted keys.
The head of the list is the next key to evict.
invariant.why: get/put move the node to the front; eviction removes the tail.

time.why: Hash lookup plus constant pointer updates.

space.why: One node and one map entry per cached key.

wrong: Heaps give the most recently used key only.
A heap would need the capacity to be a power of two.

approach: get: if absent −1; else move node to front, return value. put: update + move to front, or insert at front; if size > capacity remove tail node and its map entry.

title: Design Hit Counter
statement: Design a counter with hit(timestamp) and getHits(timestamp) returning the number of hits in the past 5 minutes (300 seconds). Calls arrive in chronological order.

nearMiss.why: Timestamps already arrive in order; a heap adds O(log n) for nothing.
Prefix counts over all time grow without bound; only the last 300 seconds matter.
Binary search over a growing list works, but old hits are never discarded and memory grows forever.

trigger.why: A count over a moving time window with in-order arrivals ⇒ queue that drops expired timestamps (or a 300-slot circular buffer).

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<Integer> of timestamps (or int[300] times + int[300] counts circular buffer)
wrong: HashMap<Integer, Integer> timestamp → count for all time
ds.why: Chronological order makes the oldest hit always at the front.

invariant.answer: After evicting from the front, the queue holds exactly the hits with timestamp > now − 300.
wrong: The queue holds the 300 most recent hits.
The queue is sorted by count.
Hits are evicted when the queue is full.
invariant.why: getHits returns the queue size after eviction.

time.answer: O(1) amortised per call (circular buffer: O(300) = O(1) per getHits)
time.why: Each hit is enqueued and evicted once.

space.answer: O(hits in the window) (circular buffer: O(300))

wrong: A heap would count hits twice.
Heaps only work when hits arrive out of order.

approach: hit: offer timestamp. getHits: while front ≤ timestamp − 300 poll; return size. (Or bucket by timestamp % 300, resetting a bucket when its stored time is stale.)

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
statement: Design a set supporting insert(val), remove(val) and getRandom() returning a uniformly random element, each in average O(1) time.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet inserts and removes in O(1), but has no O(1) way to pick a random element.
A linked list removes in O(1) given the node, but random access is O(n).
A sorted structure gives O(log n), not O(1), and random access by rank needs extra work.

trigger.why: Random access needs an array; O(1) removal from an array needs value → index + swap-with-last ⇒ ArrayList + HashMap.

ds.answer: ArrayList<Integer> values + HashMap<Integer, Integer> value → index
ds.why: Remove: move the last element into the removed slot, update its index, drop the last slot.

invariant.answer: map.get(v) is v's current index in the list, and the list has no gaps.
wrong: Removed values stay in the list as null.
The map stores counts of each value.
invariant.why: No gaps means random index in [0, size) is uniform.

time.why: Hash ops plus O(1) array swap and removal at the end.

wrong: A HashSet allows duplicates, which breaks uniformity.

approach: insert: if absent, map.put(val, list.size()); list.add(val). remove: idx = map.get(val); last = list.get(end); list.set(idx, last); map.put(last, idx); remove end; map.remove(val). getRandom: list.get(random index).

title: Snapshot Array
statement: Design an array of a given length supporting set(index, val), snap() returning a snapshot id, and get(index, snap_id) returning the value at index when that snapshot was taken. Many snaps may occur with few sets.

nearMiss.why: A map per snapshot copies the whole array on each snap: O(length) per snap.
No sums are involved; you need the latest version at or before a snapshot.
A heap gives the newest version, not the newest one ≤ snap_id.

wrong: Many snaps may occur with few sets
trigger.why: Per-index version history queried at a point in time ⇒ store (snapId, value) per index and floor-search by snapId.

ds.answer: TreeMap<Integer, Integer>[] (snapId → value per index) using floorEntry, or List<int[]> per index + binary search
wrong: int[][] full copy of the array per snap
HashMap<Integer, Integer> index → latest value only
ds.why: Only changed indices store versions; floorEntry(snapId) finds the right one.

invariant.answer: For each index, versions are stored with increasing snap ids, and the floor of snap_id is the answer.
wrong: Versions are stored newest first and the first one is returned.
invariant.why: Set overwrites the version for the current (not yet taken) snap id.

time.answer: set O(log s), snap O(1), get O(log s), s = versions at that index
wrong: get O(1) with a full copy and set O(1)
time.why: Floor lookup per get; snap just increments a counter.

wrong: Hash maps can't store snapshot ids.
Hashing would return the oldest value.
Hash maps are O(log n) per lookup.

approach: Per index keep a TreeMap snapId → value (seed {0: 0}). set: map[index].put(snapId, val). snap: return snapId++. get: map[index].floorEntry(snap_id).getValue().

title: First Missing Positive
statement: Given an unsorted integer array, return the smallest positive integer that does not appear in it. You must run in O(n) time and use O(1) auxiliary space.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet answers it in O(n) time, but uses O(n) space; the constraint is O(1).
Sorting first is O(n log n).
XOR finds a single missing value in a full range; here values can be anything, with duplicates and negatives.

trigger.why: The answer is in 1..n+1, so values can be placed at index value − 1 in the array itself. O(n) + O(1) space ⇒ cyclic sort / index marking.

ds.answer: The input int[] itself (swap each value v to index v − 1)
ds.why: The array is the hash table; no extra memory.

invariant.answer: After placement, for every v in 1..n present in the array, nums[v − 1] == v.
wrong: The array ends up fully sorted.
Negative numbers are moved to the front.
invariant.why: The first index i with nums[i] != i + 1 gives the answer i + 1 (or n + 1).

time.why: Each swap puts one value in its final place, so at most n swaps in total.

wrong: A HashSet can't store negative numbers.
A HashSet would return the largest missing value.

approach: For each i: while 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ n and nums[nums[i] − 1] != nums[i], swap them. Then return the first i + 1 with nums[i] != i + 1, else n + 1.

title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
statement: An array of n integers has values in the range 1..n; some appear twice and others not at all. Return all values in 1..n that do not appear, without extra space (the output doesn't count) in O(n) time.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet or boolean[] works in O(n) but uses O(n) extra space.
XOR tricks find one missing value, not several.
There's no sorted order or pair condition; the values map to indices.

trigger.why: Values in 1..n for length n ⇒ use index v − 1 as the 'seen' flag (negate it) or cyclic-sort.

ds.answer: The input int[] with sign marking (nums[|v| − 1] made negative)
ds.why: Signs store a bit per index without extra memory.

invariant.answer: nums[i] is negative iff value i + 1 has been seen.
wrong: nums[i] is negative iff nums[i] was originally negative.
The array is sorted after marking.
invariant.why: Unmarked (positive) indices at the end are the missing values.

time.why: Two passes.

wrong: A HashSet can't hold duplicates, so it fails here.
Hashing would need the array sorted.
A HashSet can't return missing values.

approach: For each v: idx = |v| − 1; nums[idx] = −|nums[idx]|. Collect i + 1 for every nums[i] > 0.

title: Single Number
statement: In a non-empty array, every element appears twice except for one. Find that single one using linear time and constant extra space.

nearMiss.why: A count map or set finds it in O(n), but uses O(n) space; constant space is required.
Sorting/partitioning to pair duplicates costs O(n log n) or mutates the array.
Values aren't guaranteed to be in 1..n, so they can't be placed by index.

trigger.answer: every element appears twice except for one
trigger.why: Pairs cancel under XOR (x ^ x = 0), leaving the single element.

ds.answer: One int accumulator using ^
ds.why: XOR is associative and commutative, so order doesn't matter.

invariant.answer: acc equals the XOR of all elements processed so far, so every complete pair has cancelled.
wrong: acc is the largest element seen.
acc is the sum of elements modulo 2.
acc holds the last duplicated value.
invariant.why: At the end only the unpaired value remains.

time.why: One pass.

wrong: A HashMap can't count negative numbers.
A HashMap would return the most frequent element.

approach: acc = 0; for x: acc ^= x; return acc.

twists.change: The other values may appear any number of times (two or three).
twists.statement: In an integer array exactly one value appears once; every other value appears either two or three times. Return the value that appears once.

nearMiss.why: XOR cancels pairs only, and mod-3 bit counts cancel triples only; a mix of twos and threes breaks both.
Sorting then scanning runs works, but costs O(n log n).
Partitioning doesn't isolate a count-of-one value.

twists.why: No algebraic cancellation fits mixed multiplicities ⇒ count occurrences.
twists.approach: Count every value; return the one with count 1.

title: Counting Bits
statement: Given n, return an array where entry i is the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of i, for every i from 0 to n, in O(n) total time.

nearMiss.why: Memoising counts in a map adds overhead; the recurrence only looks at a smaller index.
There are no choices to explore.
Nothing is being searched; each answer is derived from a smaller number.

trigger.answer: number of 1 bits in the binary representation
wrong: for every i from 0 to n
trigger.why: Bit counts ⇒ bit manipulation; reusing smaller answers (i >> 1) makes it O(n).

ds.answer: int[n + 1] where bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
wrong: String binary forms counted char by char
ds.why: Dropping the last bit gives a smaller, already-computed number.

invariant.answer: bits[j] is final for every j < i before bits[i] is computed.
wrong: bits[i] is the position of the highest set bit.
bits is filled from n down to 0.
invariant.why: i >> 1 < i, so the recurrence only reads finished entries.

time.why: O(1) per entry. (Integer.bitCount per i is O(n log n) in principle.)

wrong: Hash maps can't store bit counts.
Hashing would need n to be a power of two.
A map can't hold more than 32 entries.

approach: bits[0] = 0; for i in 1..n: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1).

title: Rotate Image
statement: Rotate an n × n matrix by 90 degrees clockwise in place, without allocating another matrix.

nearMiss.why: Nothing is explored; every cell moves to a fixed new position.
Reversing rows uses two pointers, but the core is the transpose + reverse index transformation.
No values are computed from neighbours; it's a permutation of cells.

trigger.why: In-place 2D index transformation ⇒ transpose then reverse each row (or rotate four cells per layer).

ds.answer: The int[][] itself with index swaps
wrong: HashMap<Integer, Integer> old index → new index
ds.why: In place by definition.

invariant.answer: After the transpose, m[i][j] holds the original m[j][i]; reversing each row then puts every value at its rotated position.
wrong: Each row is reversed before transposing for clockwise rotation.
Only the outer layer needs moving.
The diagonal elements move to the corners.
invariant.why: Clockwise: (i, j) → (j, n − 1 − i) = transpose followed by a row reversal.

time.why: Each cell moved a constant number of times.

wrong: BFS needs the matrix to be sorted.

approach: Transpose (swap m[i][j] and m[j][i] for j > i), then reverse every row.

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: Given an m × n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order: across the top row, down the right column, back along the bottom, up the left, and inwards.

nearMiss.why: A DFS with a direction rule can simulate it, but shrinking four boundaries is the clean O(1)-space approach.
There are no levels from a root; the order is a fixed walk around layers.
No nesting or LIFO order is involved.

trigger.why: Layer-by-layer walk ⇒ four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right) that shrink after each side.

ds.answer: Four int boundaries + List<Integer> output
wrong: boolean[m][n] visited with a direction array
ds.why: Boundaries replace a visited grid.

invariant.answer: Every cell outside [top..bottom] × [left..right] has already been output exactly once.
wrong: top and bottom move together every step.
Each layer has exactly four elements.
invariant.why: Re-check top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right before the bottom and left passes (non-square matrices).

time.why: Each cell once.

wrong: DFS can't move in four directions.
DFS only works on square matrices.
DFS would visit the matrix row by row.

approach: While top ≤ bottom and left ≤ right: walk top row → top++; right column → right--; if top ≤ bottom walk bottom row backwards → bottom--; if left ≤ right walk left column upwards → left++.

title: Sort Colors
statement: An array holds only the values 0, 1 and 2 (red, white, blue). Sort it in place so equal colours are adjacent in the order 0, 1, 2, in a single pass with O(1) extra space.

nearMiss.why: Counting each colour then rewriting (counting sort) takes two passes; the follow-up asks for one.
Two pointers partition into two groups; three groups need a third pointer (low / mid / high).
A heap sort is O(n log n) and not single-pass.

trigger.why: Three categories partitioned in one pass in place ⇒ Dutch national flag.

ds.answer: Three int indices (low, mid, high) on the array
ds.why: Counts work in two passes; the three pointers do it in one.

invariant.answer: [0, low) are 0s, [low, mid) are 1s, (high, end] are 2s, and [mid, high] is unprocessed.
wrong: low and high always move together.
mid advances after swapping with high.
invariant.why: After swapping with high, the new nums[mid] is unchecked, so mid stays.

time.why: One pass.

wrong: Counting would change the colours' values.

approach: low = mid = 0, high = n − 1. While mid ≤ high: 0 → swap(low++, mid++); 1 → mid++; 2 → swap(mid, high--).

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Given a string s, return the longest substring of s that reads the same forwards and backwards.

nearMiss.why: Palindromes aren't monotonic: a longer window can be a palindrome when a shorter one isn't.
Converging pointers check ONE given string; finding the longest needs expansion from every centre.
A stack reverses, but checking every substring with it is O(n³).

trigger.answer: reads the same forwards and backwards
trigger.why: Palindromic substrings grow symmetrically from a centre ⇒ expand around each of the 2n − 1 centres.

ds.answer: Two int indices per centre; track best start and length
ds.why: The DP table works but uses O(n²) space; expansion needs O(1).

invariant.answer: While expanding, s[l..r] is a palindrome centred on the current centre.
wrong: l and r always move in the same direction.
The best palindrome always contains s[0].
invariant.why: Stop as soon as s[l] != s[r]; the palindrome is s[l + 1..r − 1].

time.why: 2n − 1 centres, each expanding up to O(n). (Manacher: O(n).)

wrong: A window needs the string sorted.
Sliding window only finds even-length palindromes.

approach: For each centre c (odd: c, c; even: c, c + 1) expand while s[l] == s[r]; keep the longest span.

twists.change: The palindrome may skip characters (subsequence, not substring).
twists.statement: Given a string, return the length of its longest palindromic subsequence: characters kept in order, but not necessarily adjacent.

nearMiss.why: Expanding from a centre only grows contiguous palindromes; a subsequence can skip characters on either side.
A single pass from both ends can't decide which side to skip on a mismatch; both branches matter.
Enumerating subsequences is exponential; the (i, j) states overlap.

twists.why: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1] + 2 if s[i] == s[j], else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]). (Equivalently LCS of s and its reverse.)
twists.approach: Fill dp by increasing length (or i from n − 1 down, j from i up). Return dp[0][n − 1].

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement: Given a string, count how many of its substrings are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately even if equal.

nearMiss.why: Hashing distinct substrings loses the 'different positions count separately' rule and is still O(n²) substrings.
Partitioning into palindromes is a different problem; here you just count substrings.
There's no numeric sum to difference.

trigger.why: Every palindrome has a centre; each successful expansion step is one more palindrome ⇒ expand around centres and count.

ds.answer: Two int indices per centre and a counter
ds.why: Counting during expansion needs no storage.

invariant.answer: Each step where s[l] == s[r] while expanding from a centre adds exactly one new palindrome.
wrong: Each centre contributes exactly one palindrome.
Only palindromes longer than 1 are counted.
invariant.why: Different (centre, radius) pairs are different positions.

time.why: 2n − 1 centres × O(n) expansion.

wrong: Hashing would count single letters twice.
A HashSet needs the string sorted.

approach: For every centre (odd and even) expand while characters match, incrementing the count each step.

title: Replace Words
statement: Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence by the shortest root it starts with (words with no matching root stay as they are). Return the new sentence.

nearMiss.why: Sorting roots and binary-searching a word finds neighbours, not the SHORTEST root that is a prefix; you'd still check several candidates.
Prefixes all start at the word's first character; there's no window that slides.
Comparing a word against every root with two indices is O(words × roots × length).

trigger.answer: the shortest root it starts with
trigger.why: Shortest dictionary prefix of each word ⇒ walk the word down a trie and stop at the first end-of-word marker.

ds.answer: Trie of roots (TrieNode[26] children + boolean isEnd), plus StringBuilder output
ds.why: A HashSet of roots and trying each prefix length also works (O(L²) per word).

invariant.answer: While walking a word, the current trie node represents the prefix read so far; the first node marked isEnd is the shortest root.
wrong: Each trie node stores a whole word.
The deepest matching node is the answer.
Words are inserted into the trie as they are replaced.
invariant.why: Stop early: no need to read the rest of the word.

wrong: O(roots log roots + words log roots)
time.why: Each character is visited a constant number of times.

wrong: Binary search would return the longest root, which is what's asked.
Binary search needs the sentence sorted.

approach: Insert roots into a trie. For each word, walk the trie: if a node is end, use that prefix; if a child is missing, keep the word.

title: Search Suggestions System
statement: Given a list of product names and a search word, after each character typed return up to three products that start with the typed prefix, in lexicographic order.

nearMiss.why: A heap per prefix would re-scan all products each keystroke; the sorted order gives the three smallest directly.
A map from every prefix to its products works but stores every prefix of every product.
The candidate range only ever narrows as you type, but it's defined by a prefix, not a count budget.

trigger.why: Prefix lookups as you type ⇒ trie with up to 3 suggestions stored per node (or sort + binary search the lower bound per prefix).

ds.answer: Trie whose nodes keep a List<String> of up to 3 words, inserted in sorted order
ds.why: Sort products first so the first three inserted into each node are the smallest.

invariant.answer: Each trie node lists the (at most 3) lexicographically smallest products having that node's prefix.
wrong: Each node stores every product with its prefix.
Suggestions are the three shortest products.
The root stores the answer for the whole word.
invariant.why: Typing walks one node per character.

time.answer: O(P log P · L) to sort, plus O(total chars) to build and O(L) to query
time.why: Sorting dominates.

wrong: Heaps return suggestions in random order.
A heap would return the three longest products.

approach: Sort products. Insert each into a trie, appending it to every node's list while the list has < 3 words. For each prefix, walk one node and output its list (empty after a missing child).

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack supporting push, pop, top and getMin, where getMin returns the smallest element currently in the stack. Every operation must run in O(1) time.

nearMiss.why: A heap gives the minimum, but popping the stack's top element from a heap is O(n) (or lazy deletion).
Popping larger elements to keep it monotonic would lose stack contents; instead remember the min alongside each entry.
There's no median or two-sided balance; only the minimum is needed.

trigger.answer: getMin returns the smallest element currently in the stack
wrong: Every operation must run in O(1) time
trigger.why: The minimum must survive pops ⇒ store 'min so far' with every entry (a parallel stack of minimums).

ds.answer: ArrayDeque<int[]> of {value, minSoFar} (or two ArrayDeque<Integer>)
wrong: TreeMap<Integer, Integer> value → count plus a stack
One int min field updated on push
ds.why: A single min field can't recover the previous minimum after a pop. TreeMap works but is O(log n).

invariant.answer: Each entry stores the minimum of itself and everything below it, so the top entry's minSoFar is the current minimum.
wrong: The minimum is always at the bottom.
getMin pops until the minimum is found.
invariant.why: Pop restores the previous minimum automatically.

time.why: Constant work per call.

wrong: A heap would return the maximum.

approach: push(x): stack.push({x, min(x, top.min)}). pop: stack.pop(). top: peek[0]. getMin: peek[1].

title: LFU Cache
statement: Design a cache with a fixed capacity supporting get and put in O(1) average time. When full, evict the key used the fewest times; among keys tied on use count, evict the least recently used.

nearMiss.why: A min-heap by (count, time) finds the victim, but every get changes a count, so updates cost O(log n), not O(1).
A map gives O(1) lookup, but on its own can't find the least-frequent, least-recent key quickly.
Doubly linked lists hold the recency order inside each frequency, but they're one part of a combined structure.

trigger.answer: the key used the fewest times
trigger.why: Evict by frequency, then recency, in O(1) ⇒ key → node map + frequency → LRU list map + a minFreq pointer.

ds.answer: HashMap<Integer, Node> keys, HashMap<Integer, LinkedHashSet<Integer>> freq → keys in recency order, int minFreq
ds.why: LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order per frequency bucket.

invariant.answer: Each key sits in exactly the bucket of its use count, ordered by recency; minFreq is the smallest non-empty bucket.
wrong: Every bucket holds at most one key.
Keys move to the bucket of count − 1 on get.
invariant.why: A new key resets minFreq to 1; a bucket emptying at minFreq bumps it by one.

time.why: Hash operations and list moves only.

space.why: Each key appears once in the maps.

wrong: A heap would evict the most frequent key.
Heaps need a fixed capacity, which LFU doesn't have.

approach: get: move key from bucket f to f + 1 (bump minFreq if bucket f emptied and f == minFreq). put: update if present; else if full evict the first key of bucket minFreq; insert with count 1, minFreq = 1.

title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
statement: An array of n integers has values in the range 1..n, and each value appears once or twice. Return every value that appears twice, in O(n) time using only constant extra space (the output doesn't count).

nearMiss.why: A HashSet finds duplicates in O(n) but needs O(n) extra space.
Floyd finds ONE duplicate; here there can be many, and the array may be modified.
XOR tricks cancel pairs; they can't list which values occurred twice.

wrong: Return every value that appears twice
trigger.why: Values 1..n map to indices 0..n−1 ⇒ use the array as its own visited set (negate nums[v − 1]).

ds.answer: The int[] itself: sign of nums[|v| − 1] marks 'seen'
ds.why: The sign bit is free storage.

invariant.answer: nums[i] is negative iff value i + 1 has been seen; meeting an already-negative slot means |v| is a duplicate.
wrong: nums is sorted after the pass.
Negative values were in the input.
Each slot is negated twice for duplicates, so it ends positive.
invariant.why: Use |nums[i]| when reading because earlier flips may have negated it.

time.why: One pass.

wrong: Hashing would find each duplicate three times.

approach: For each v: i = |v| − 1; if nums[i] < 0 add |v| to the answer; else nums[i] = −nums[i].

title: Set Mismatch
statement: An array should contain each number 1..n exactly once, but one number was replaced by a copy of another, so one value repeats and one is missing. Return [repeated, missing].

nearMiss.why: Floyd finds the repeated value but not the missing one, and here the array can be modified.
The array isn't sorted, and sorting first costs O(n log n).
Sum and sum-of-squares equations do work arithmetically, but they're a math trick, not range sums; index marking is the recognisable pattern.

wrong: one value repeats and one is missing
trigger.why: 1..n values ⇒ each value has a home index; one slot gets hit twice, one slot never.

ds.answer: The int[] itself (negate nums[|v| − 1] to mark, or swap values home)
ds.why: A HashSet / count array version is the O(n)-space alternate.

invariant.answer: After marking, a slot found already negative names the repeated value; the one slot left positive names the missing value.
wrong: The repeated value is always at index 0.
The missing value is always n.
invariant.why: Every present value marks its home index once.

time.why: Two passes.

wrong: Fast/slow pointers can't run on arrays.
Floyd needs the list to have no cycle.
Floyd would return the missing value instead.

approach: For v: i = |v| − 1; if nums[i] < 0 repeated = |v| else negate. Then the index i with nums[i] > 0 gives missing = i + 1.

title: Missing Number
statement: An array holds n distinct numbers taken from 0..n, so exactly one value in that range is absent. Return it using O(1) extra space.

nearMiss.why: A HashSet of values finds it but needs O(n) space.
Only works if the array is sorted, and sorting costs O(n log n).
There's no pair to find; the answer is one value's absence.

trigger.answer: exactly one value in that range is absent
trigger.why: Every other value appears once as an index and once as a value ⇒ XOR everything and only the missing one survives (Gauss sum also works).

ds.answer: One int accumulator with ^
ds.why: One int; n(n + 1)/2 minus the sum of the values works too.

invariant.answer: x = (0 ^ 1 ^ … ^ n) ^ (all values); every present value cancels with its index, leaving the missing one.
wrong: x is the sum of the values so far.
x always equals the largest value seen.
x is zero until the missing value is reached.
invariant.why: a ^ a = 0 and XOR is order-independent.

time.why: One pass.

wrong: Hashing would find two missing numbers.
Hashing requires values to be sorted.

approach: x = n; for i: x ^= i ^ nums[i]. Return x.

title: Single Number II
statement: In an integer array every value appears exactly three times except for one value, which appears exactly once. Find that value in linear time with constant extra space.

nearMiss.why: Counting with a map works but uses O(n) space.
Quickselect-style grouping could isolate it, but that's O(n) average with heavy bookkeeping; per-bit counting is exact and simple.
Sorting then scanning in steps of three is O(n log n).

trigger.why: Plain XOR cancels pairs, not triples ⇒ count each bit position mod 3 (or the ones/twos bitmask state machine).

ds.answer: Two int bitmasks ones and twos (or a loop over 32 bit counts)
ds.why: A single XOR would leave the triples' bits set.

invariant.answer: For every bit position, the count of 1s across the array is ≡ the single value's bit (mod 3).
wrong: XOR of all values equals the single value.
The single value is the smallest in the array.
Each bit is set in at most one value.
invariant.why: Bits of the triples contribute multiples of 3.

time.answer: O(n) (32 · n with the bit-count loop)
time.why: Constant work per element per bit.

wrong: A HashMap can't count to three.
Hashing would return a value that appears three times.

approach: For bit b in 0..31: c = Σ (x >> b) & 1; if c % 3 != 0 set bit b of the answer. (Negative values work because all 32 bits are rebuilt.)

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
statement: For every 0 in an m × n integer matrix, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in place using O(1) extra space.

nearMiss.why: Sets of zero rows and columns work, but cost O(m + n) space; the follow-up wants O(1).
Zeros don't spread to neighbours repeatedly; one zero affects exactly its row and column.
There's no distance from the zeros; whole rows and columns flip at once.

wrong: set its entire row and column to 0
trigger.why: Row/column flags in O(1) space ⇒ store them in the first row and column, with two booleans for the first row/column themselves.

ds.answer: The matrix's first row and column as marker arrays, plus two booleans
ds.why: Markers live inside the matrix.

invariant.answer: matrix[r][0] == 0 marks row r and matrix[0][c] == 0 marks column c; the first row/column are zeroed last so markers aren't lost.
wrong: Zeroing happens as soon as a 0 is found.
The first row is always zeroed.
Only the first zero found matters.
invariant.why: Zeroing early would create fake zeros that spread.

time.why: Two passes over the matrix.

wrong: A HashSet can't store row numbers.
Hashing would zero the wrong cells.

approach: Record whether row 0 / column 0 contain a 0. Mark matrix[r][0] and matrix[0][c] for every inner zero. Zero inner cells whose row or column is marked. Finally zero row 0 / column 0 if flagged.

title: Game of Life
statement: Each cell of a board is live (1) or dead (0). Compute the next generation by the usual neighbour-count rules (all eight neighbours, all cells updating simultaneously), updating the board in place.

nearMiss.why: There's no search: each cell is updated from its eight neighbours exactly once.
Changes don't propagate outward; every cell is decided by the previous generation only.
A cell's new state depends on the OLD neighbours, not on already-computed new ones.

trigger.why: Simultaneous update in place ⇒ encode old and new state in the same cell (e.g. bit 0 = old, bit 1 = new) and shift at the end.

ds.answer: The board itself with two bits per cell (old state in bit 0, next state in bit 1)
wrong: A full copy of the board
ds.why: A copy is O(m · n) space; bit encoding is O(1).

invariant.answer: During the pass, every cell's bit 0 still holds the current generation, so neighbour counts read (cell & 1).
wrong: Cells already visited hold only the next generation.
Live counts are taken from bit 1.
Cells are updated in order of their neighbour count.
invariant.why: Final pass: cell >>= 1.

time.why: Eight neighbours per cell.

wrong: BFS would update cells one generation too late.
Grid BFS only works with four neighbours.

approach: For each cell count live neighbours with (cell & 1). Set bit 1 if (live and 2–3 neighbours) or (dead and 3). Then shift every cell right by 1.

title: Sort Array By Parity
statement: Rearrange an integer array in place so that every even number comes before every odd number. Any such arrangement is acceptable.

nearMiss.why: There's no choice to optimise; it's a two-way partition by a predicate.
Sorting by parity with a comparator is O(n log n); a partition is O(n).
Values don't have home indices; only their parity class matters.

trigger.answer: every even number comes before every odd number
trigger.why: Split by a predicate in place, order within groups irrelevant ⇒ partition (Lomuto/Hoare style).

ds.answer: The int[] itself with a boundary index (Lomuto) or two converging indices (Hoare)
wrong: int[] counts of evens and odds
ds.why: O(1) space.

invariant.answer: nums[0..boundary) are all even; everything between boundary and the scan index is odd.
wrong: boundary always equals the number of odds seen.
invariant.why: When the scan finds an even, swap it to the boundary and advance the boundary.

time.why: One pass.

wrong: Greedy would sort the numbers by value.
Greedy needs the array sorted first.

approach: b = 0; for i: if nums[i] % 2 == 0 swap(nums, i, b++).

title: Wiggle Sort II
statement: Reorder an integer array so that nums[0] < nums[1] > nums[2] < nums[3]…, strictly alternating. Values may repeat. Follow-up: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

nearMiss.why: Swapping neighbours that break the pattern works only for ≤ / ≥ (Wiggle Sort I); with strict inequalities and duplicates it fails.
A heap can produce sorted halves in O(n log n), missing the O(n) follow-up.
Sorting then interleaving the halves (reversed) is the O(n log n) solution; the O(n) one needs the median and a 3-way partition.

trigger.answer: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
trigger.why: Large values on odd indices and small on even, without sorting ⇒ quickselect the median, then 3-way (Dutch flag) partition through a virtual index mapping.

ds.answer: The int[] itself: quickselect for the median, then Dutch flag with index map (1 + 2i) % (n | 1)
wrong: Sorted copy split into two halves
ds.why: The sorted-copy version is O(n) space and O(n log n) time.

invariant.answer: Through the virtual index mapping, values > median fill odd slots first and values < median fill even slots from the end, so equal-to-median values are kept apart.
wrong: Each pair (i, i + 1) is sorted ascending.
The median ends up at index n / 2.
invariant.why: The mapping visits odd indices first, then even ones.

time.why: Quickselect plus one partition pass.

space.why: In place (the sorting variant needs O(n)).

wrong: Greedy would need the array sorted descending.
Greedy only works for odd n.

approach: m = quickselect median. Dutch flag over virtual index A(i) = (1 + 2i) % (n | 1): > m swap to the left region, < m swap to the right region, == m advance.
